findings.summary: A `${window.…}` template name that this window mode cannot supply is accepted, because the message is inside `void (...)` instead of `refuse`, so the field always renders as absent.
findings.failure_scenario: A first-window handler with emit {x: '${window.count}'} compiles; field x is omitted from every row, and the test expects /not available/.

findings.summary: A `calls` window closes as soon as an event past the limit arrives. It never checks the `running` set (which nothing reads), although the contract says it must stay open while any call within the limit is unfinished.
findings.failure_scenario: calls:1, trigger call 5. Call 6 starts, then call 7 starts and emits an event before call 6 ends. The window closes as 'calls' (counted as noMatch) and call 6's later matching end event is lost.

findings.summary: A `calls` window closes on the first event past the limit without checking `running`, so a call inside the limit that is still unfinished loses its late events, contrary to the runHandler contract.
findings.failure_scenario: calls: 1 from call 1. Call 3 starts and ends before call 2 ends. Call 3's event closes the window (n=0, or 1 depending on ordering), and call 2's late command.run, which is inside the limit, is dropped. The test 'holds a calls window open while a call inside the limit is still running' expects n=1.

findings.summary: A `calls`-only window closes by 'calls' only when a later event past the limit arrives; if the last in-limit call finishes and the next event is `session.end`, the session.end branch wins and the window is counted as unclosed rather than decided.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: {calls: 1, absent: {...}}`, the trigger's call+1 starts and ends, then the stream ends: close() sees closedBy='session.end' with until undefined and increments `unclosed` instead of emitting the absent row (or, for `first`, `noMatch`).

findings.summary: A `capture.<name>` with no explicit `group:` defaults to group 1, but nothing checks that the compiled regex actually has a capturing group, so a groupless regex produces a capture that is always silently absent.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler author writes `capture: { tag: { field: 'head', regex: 'bash' } }` (no `group:` key, and the regex 'bash' has zero capturing groups), expecting `${tag}` in `emit` to hold 'bash' whenever `head` matches. compileHandler accepts it; at runtime `capture.regex.exec(source)` returns a match array with no index 1, so `found?.[capture.group]` is always `undefined` and `fields.tag` never appears on any emitted row -- the handler compiles cleanly and runs 'green' while a declared field is silently absent forever, which is exactly the class of mistake this file's own header says is refused everywhere ('a handler that matches nothing looks exactly like a handler with nothing to match ... every such mistake is refused here'). Confirmed empirically: the spec above run against a matching command.run event emits a row whose `fields` contains `x: 'ran'` but no `tag` key at all.

findings.summary: A `first` or `count` window with `until: session.end` that ends without a match is counted `unclosed`. The `absent` sibling treats the same end as a decided verdict.
findings.failure_scenario: `until: 'session.end', first: {on: 'command.run'}` with no command before the stream ends goes to `unclosed += 1` (also line 1105 for count). The `absent` branch (line 1112) exempts `spec.until === 'session.end'`. The 'no match' verdict is therefore reported as undecided, and the `noMatch` counter under-reports.

findings.summary: A `session.end` event closes every open window even under `scope: session`, despite the comment saying it must never close a session's windows.
findings.failure_scenario: Handler with `scope: session`, `window: {until: agent.return, first: {...}}`. A subagent's stream emits its own `session.end` while the main stream's window is still waiting. `closedBy = 'session.end'` is set unconditionally, so every window in the session is closed and counted `unclosed`, and later matches never emit. Only the `open.delete` at 1223 is guarded by scope, not this close.

findings.summary: A `where` (or an any/all element, or a `not` operand) that is not a map compiles to a test that is always true instead of being refused.
findings.failure_scenario: where: 'head == bd' or any: ['x'] compiles to match every event, so the handler emits a row for every trigger instead of refusing the mistake.

findings.summary: A `where` (or an any/all/not element) that is not a map compiles to an always-true test instead of being refused.
findings.failure_scenario: where: 'command' or where: ['x'] or not: 5 compiles; the top-level where then matches every event of the kind, and `not: 5` becomes always false.

findings.summary: A capture `group` beyond the regex's number of groups is not validated, so the capture is never set.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: {a: {field: 'tool', regex: '(B)', group: 3}}` compiles. At line 1235 `found?.[3]` is always undefined, so `a` is never captured. Any `$a` condition is never true and `${a}` is omitted from every row. Nothing is refused, despite the file's strict-load design.

findings.summary: A capture `group` index is validated only as a non-negative integer, not against the number of groups in the compiled regex.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: { id: { field: cmd, regex: 'run (\\w+)', group: 2 } }` compiles. `found?.[2]` is always undefined, so the capture is never set. `${id}` is absent on every row and `$id` conditions are never true. The handler loads and runs green with no message.

findings.summary: A capture `group` is validated only as a non-negative integer, not against the number of groups in the compiled regex.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: {to: {field:'after', regex:'Status:\\s*(\\w+)', group: 2}}` compiles. At runtime `found?.[2]` is undefined, so the capture is never set, and `$to: {exists: true}` is never true. The handler matches nothing with no error.

findings.summary: A capture is refused for shadowing only array fields (`=== 'array'`), while each.as (line 855) refuses any existing field (`!== undefined`).
findings.failure_scenario: capture: {command: {field: command, regex: '(\w+)'}} compiles; `$command` and `${command}` now return the capture, not the field, and refType types it as a string whatever the field's type.

findings.summary: A capture only refuses shadowing a trigger field of type array, while `each.as` refuses shadowing any field (line 855); the message claims any field.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: {path: {field: command, regex: ...}}` on an event with a string `path` field. The scope resolves the captured value first, so `${path}` and `where: {$path: ...}` silently read the capture instead of the event's real `path`. A number-typed source field also passes the string-field check and the capture is silently skipped.

findings.summary: A capture whose regex does not match is stored as '' (present), while a capture whose source field is absent is left unset (absent).
findings.failure_scenario: For a single-reference template `${cap}`, a non-matching command emits an empty string, while an event with no source field omits the field. The file elsewhere says absent and empty are different facts, and `where: {$cap: {exists: false}}` cannot detect a non-match.

findings.summary: A capture whose regex does not match is stored as '' rather than left absent, although templates treat absent and empty as different facts; a non-string source instead falls through to the event field.
findings.failure_scenario: capture id with regex 'bd-(\d+)' on a command without 'bd-' emits fields.id = '' rather than omitting it, and `$id eq ''` style conditions match.

findings.summary: A capture whose regex does not match is stored as the empty string, but a capture whose source field is missing stays absent, so `exists` and single-reference templates treat 'no match' as present.
findings.failure_scenario: capture to: {field:'after', regex:'Status:(\w+)'} on an event whose `after` lacks 'Status:': `$to: {exists: true}` is true and `${to}` emits '' instead of being omitted, which contradicts the file's rule that absent and empty are different facts.

findings.summary: A capture whose regex does not match, or whose `group` exceeds the regex's group count, is stored as '' instead of being left absent.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: {id: {field: 'cmd', regex: 'x(\\d+)'}}` on cmd 'ls'. `captured.id` is '', so `${id}` emits an empty string and `exists` is true. The template comment says absent and empty are different facts. `group: 5` on a 1-group regex is not refused at compile time and yields '' on every event.

findings.summary: A capture's `group` is never checked against the number of groups in its regex, so a group past the last one is always undefined and the capture is silently never set.
findings.failure_scenario: capture `{regex: 'a(b)', group: 2}` compiles; every `$name` reference is then absent, and `eq` conditions on it are silently never true.

findings.summary: A count window emits only when `count > atLeast`, but at_least means a minimum reached (count >= at_least). The default of 0 at line 736 encodes the same off-by-one.
findings.failure_scenario: With at_least: 2 and exactly 2 repeats, count 2 > 2 is false, so the row is counted as noMatch instead of emitted. The 'count: emits at close only when at_least is reached' test expects [[1,'2']] and fails. Fixing to >= requires the default to become 1, otherwise a window with 0 matches would emit.

findings.summary: A count window emits only when `count > atLeast`, so `at_least: N` needs N+1 matches. The default of 0 (line 736) only works because of the same off-by-one.
findings.failure_scenario: With `at_least: 2` and a trigger that sees exactly 2 repeats, the window closes with 2 > 2 false and counts as noMatch instead of emitting. The test 'count: emits at close only when at_least is reached' expects call 1 to emit with 2 repeats. The fix is `>=` together with a default of 1, so that the 'still emits a count that reached at_least' test keeps the empty-count window undecided.

findings.summary: A count window emits only when `count > atLeast`, so reaching exactly `at_least` counts as a miss.
findings.failure_scenario: at_least: 2 with exactly 2 repeats counts as noMatch and emits nothing (the 'count: emits at close only when at_least is reached' test expects [[1,'2']]); with the default at_least 0, a count of 0 never emits.

findings.summary: A line whose kind is id-bearing but whose id is not a string is reported as 'unknown "kind"', naming the wrong field in the problem string a caller fixes a tree from.
findings.failure_scenario: The record {"kind":"entry","id":7} is refused with problem: 'not a record line (unknown "kind")'. The kind IS known; the id is what is unusable. The file's docblock promises the problem string is what the caller acts on.

findings.summary: A non-string `description` is not refused (the message is inside `void`) and is then cast to `string | undefined` in the compiled handler.
findings.failure_scenario: description: 42 compiles, and `handler.description` is the number 42 although it is typed as string, so a caller calling `.trim()` on it throws.

findings.summary: A non-string `description` is not refused (the statement is `void`) but is then cast to `string | undefined`.
findings.failure_scenario: description: 42 or {a:1} compiles, and CompiledHandler.description holds a number or object typed as a string, which breaks consumers that call string methods on it.

findings.summary: A non-string `description` is not refused: the message is inside `void (...)`, and the value is then cast to `string | undefined`.
findings.failure_scenario: `description: 42` or `description: [a]` compiles, and `CompiledHandler.description` holds a number or array despite its `string | undefined` type, so downstream string operations misbehave.

findings.summary: A record file sitting directly under `entries/` or `annotations/` rather than in a partition is silently ignored, contradicting the module's documented claim that a line in the wrong place is always refused.
findings.failure_scenario: `writeFileSync(root + '/entries/0001.jsonl', <one valid entry line>)` then `readRecordTree(root)` returns 0 lines and no error. The loop descends only through `partitionNamesIn`, which filters to directories, so a file at the top of a partitioned kind is never opened. Reachable via a hand edit or a mis-targeted `git mv` or merge-tool move.

findings.summary: A reference that does not fully match the template regex is emitted as literal text instead of being refused, which lets a typo through unnoticed.
findings.failure_scenario: emit {x: '${head|Upper}'}, '${head | basename}' or '${head|}' compiles without error, and every row emits the literal string '${head|Upper}' instead of the value or an 'unknown filter' refusal.

findings.summary: A regex is refused when `source.length >= MAX_REGEX_LENGTH`, but the docs say 'longer than this is refused', so a source of exactly 300 characters is refused too.
findings.failure_scenario: A 300-character regex is rejected with 'regex is 300 characters, over 300'.

findings.summary: A stream's `session.end` clears `open` and `running` for the key but not `lastBefore`, so the last `before:` match survives the stream's end.
findings.failure_scenario: A stream key `(session, agent)` that appears again after `session.end` (resumed or re-read transcript) gets its first trigger joined to a `before` event from the ended stream. That trigger is not counted in `unsatisfiedBefore`. The map also grows by one entry per stream that ever ended.

findings.summary: A stream's `session.end` clears `open` and `running` for the partition but not `lastBefore`, so a `before:` reference survives the end of its stream.
findings.failure_scenario: Two transcript files with the same (session_id, agent_id) (e.g. a resumed stream) replayed in sequence: the first trigger of the second file resolves `${before.*}` to an event from the ended stream and `unsatisfiedBefore` is under-counted.

findings.summary: A stream's session.end deletes its `open` and `running` entries but not its `lastBefore` entry, so before-references outlive their stream and the map grows with every stream until finish().
findings.failure_scenario: On a live run over many streams with a before: handler, lastBefore keeps one event per ended stream indefinitely, so memory grows with no bound, contrary to the 'BOUNDED' design claim. If a (session_id, agent_id) key recurs (for example a resumed transcript), its first trigger resolves ${before.*} to an event from the previous stream instead of counting unsatisfiedBefore.

findings.summary: A stream's session.end deletes its open windows and running calls but not its lastBefore entry, so a `before:` reference outlives the stream end and can join across it.
findings.failure_scenario: Stream s1/main: file.changed /a.ts, session.end, then (resumed transcript, same key) check.run → row carries prior '/a.ts' from the ended segment instead of absent+unsatisfiedBefore; the map also retains one event per ended stream until finish().

findings.summary: A stream's session.end deletes its open windows and running calls but not its lastBefore entry, so the before reference outlives the stream and accumulates across all streams until finish().
findings.failure_scenario: A long replay over many sessions retains one event per stream ever seen; if a stream key recurs (resumed session with same session_id/agent_id), its first trigger resolves ${before.*} to an event from the previous, ended stream instead of counting unsatisfiedBefore.

findings.summary: A stream's session.end deletes its open windows and running calls but not its lastBefore entry, so the before-reference survives the end of the stream.
findings.failure_scenario: If the same (session_id, agent_id) is replayed again (a resumed or second transcript file), the first trigger resolves ${before.path} to an event from the previous, ended stream instead of being counted in unsatisfiedBefore. The entry also stays in memory until finish().

findings.summary: A stream-scoped window with neither `calls` nor `until` is not refused (the refusal is `void`), though the session branch refuses an unbounded window and the message says it is never decided.
findings.failure_scenario: window: {first: {on: tool.use.end}} under scope stream compiles; windows never close by a bound and only turn into unclosed at session.end.

findings.summary: A stream-scoped window with neither `calls` nor `until` is not refused, because the message is wrapped in `void (...)` instead of `refuse(...)`, so the window has no end.
findings.failure_scenario: window: {first: {on: 'command.run'}} compiles; its windows close only at session.end and are counted as unclosed. The handler never decides anything, and the test expects /never decided/.

findings.summary: A template reference whose filter is not `[a-z_]+` (e.g. uppercase, digits, empty) or that is malformed simply fails the reference regex and is emitted verbatim as literal text instead of being refused.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: { x: '${head|Upper}' }` or `'${head|}'` compiles (no 'unknown filter' refusal) and every row carries the literal string "${head|Upper}"; `'${head'` likewise emits literally.

findings.summary: A throwing readdirSync is treated as 'nothing here' for every errno, not just ENOENT, and the log source never reports its failures where the transcript source reports unreadable.
findings.failure_scenario: An events/<session>/<agent>/ directory is unreadable (EACCES) or a path component is a file (ENOTDIR). The replay reports an undercounted handler count with unreadable: 0. typed-handlers.ts:108 is the sibling that discriminates ENOENT explicitly.

findings.summary: An `absent` window decided by a match is removed with no row and no counter increment, so triggers ≠ rows + unclosed + noMatch for absent handlers — the same silence noMatch was added to close.
findings.failure_scenario: absent handler: file.read, then matching file.changed, then session.end → triggers=1, rows=0, unclosed=0, noMatch=0; a reader cannot tell this trigger from one that never opened a window.

findings.summary: An invalid regex is swallowed and replaced by `/$^/`, which never matches, instead of being refused.
findings.failure_scenario: `matches: '('` or flags `ii` (accepted by REGEX_FLAGS but rejected by RegExp) compiles to a never-matching pattern. A `where` is silently never true, and a `not:` around it is always true. This is the exact silent-wrong-handler class the file says it refuses. It also leaves the `error` binding unused and does not throw `HandlerError`.

findings.summary: An invalid regex is swallowed in the catch and replaced with `/$^/`, which never matches. The handler compiles but is silently never true.
findings.failure_scenario: `where: {cmd: {matches: '(unclosed'}}` makes `new RegExp` throw. Instead of a refusal, the compiler substitutes a never-matching pattern. The handler loads and produces zero rows, the exact class the file header says is refused. The `error` variable is also unused.

findings.summary: An invalid regex source is caught and quietly replaced with `/$^/`, which never matches, when it should be refused.
findings.failure_scenario: where: {command: {matches: '(unclosed'}} compiles without error, and the condition is false for every event, so the handler matches nothing with no error.

findings.summary: An invalid regex source is swallowed in the catch and replaced with `/$^/`, which never matches, so the handler loads and silently matches nothing.
findings.failure_scenario: where: {head: {matches: '('}} compiles fine and every event fails the condition; nothing is emitted and there is no error (the test expects 'Invalid regular expression').

findings.summary: An opened window stores the raw trigger `scope` instead of `emitScope`, so `${before.…}` on a window row reads the trigger's own fields, contrary to the comment directly above.
findings.failure_scenario: Take a handler with `before: {on: file.changed}` and a window `first: {on: check.run}` that emits `r: ${before.path}`. The row has r: '' (resolved as the trigger's field `before.path`) instead of the earlier file.changed path. The test 'resolves the reference at the TRIGGER…' fails.

findings.summary: An unavailable `${window.*}` template name is not refused: the refusal message is built inside `void (...)` and the function returns normally.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: {n: '${window.count}'}` on a handler with no window, or `${window.first.x}` on a `count` window, or `${window.bogus}`, all compile. At runtime the value is undefined, so the field is silently omitted or emitted as an empty string.

findings.summary: An unavailable `${window.…}` template name is discarded with `void` instead of refused, unlike the `before.` branch just above, which refuses.
findings.failure_scenario: emit: {n: '${window.count}'} on a first-mode window (or ${window.first.x} on count mode, or no window) compiles, and the field is silently absent on every row.

findings.summary: An unavailable `window.*` template name is not refused. The refusal message is wrapped in `void (...)` and the function returns.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: {n: '${window.count}'}` on a `first` window, or `${window.bogus}`, compiles. At run time the scope returns undefined, so the field is silently omitted or rendered as ''. This is the never-true class the file refuses elsewhere.

findings.summary: Array values are compared by reference: `in` accepts arrays as list elements for an array field (typeOf matches 'array'), and eq/ne accept a `$ref` of array type. Set.has / === never match two different arrays, so the condition is silently never true (always true for ne).
findings.failure_scenario: `where: {argv: {in: [['git','status']]}}` on command.run compiles and never matches. A window where `{argv: {eq: $argv}}` (trigger's argv vs. the later event's argv) compiles and never matches even when both are ['npm','test']. Nothing is refused and zero rows come out.

findings.summary: At a stream's session.end the code removes `open` and `running` for the partition but leaves `lastBefore`, so a before reference outlives the stream and the map grows without bound across streams until finish().
findings.failure_scenario: If a stream key appears again after its session.end (a resumed or re-read transcript), its first trigger resolves `${before.*}` to an event from the ended stream instead of counting unsatisfiedBefore.

findings.summary: Both branches of `partition` return `event.session_id`, so `scope: stream` merges every agent's stream in a session into one partition, although the docs say it partitions by `(session_id, agent_id)`.
findings.failure_scenario: A main agent and a subagent share session S. A subagent's `session.end` closes (and `open.delete`s) the main agent's open windows. Its events can also satisfy the main agent's windows, and its seq/call numbers get compared against the main stream's.

findings.summary: Both branches of `partition` return `event.session_id`, so under the default `scope: stream` every agent's stream in a session shares one partition, even though the doc and `row()` treat the partition as `(session_id, agent_id)`.
findings.failure_scenario: file.changed in (s1, main), then check.run in (s1, sub), then prompt.submit in (s1, main), run through an `absent: {on: check.run}` handler: the subagent's check.run decides main's window, so no row is emitted. The test 'keeps interleaved streams apart' expects ['a.ts']. A subagent's session.end also clears main's windows and main's before-reference.

findings.summary: Capture regexes run `exec` over the full source string. Every other regex path goes through `test()`, which truncates to MAX_SUBJECT_LENGTH, so the stated ReDoS bound does not hold for captures.
findings.failure_scenario: A 5 MB field with a backtracking capture regex is executed over all 5 MB per event. The same regex in `where` would be limited to 100,000 characters.

findings.summary: CompiledHandler.spec stores the caller's `parsed` object by reference, while hash and the compiled closures are fixed at compile time. A later mutation of the caller's object changes `spec` without changing `hash` or behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller compiles `parsed`, then edits `parsed.emit.extra = '${path}'` (or reuses the object for another handler). handler.spec now shows the extra field but handler.hash and the emitted rows still reflect the original, so the stored spec no longer matches its identity hash.

findings.summary: E12.14 Stage 1 states a headroom figure that subtracts the E12.13 header twice, contradicting the research record it descends from.
findings.failure_scenario: Stage 1's measurement was taken after E12.13, when the brief was 3,419 bytes as asc doctor counts it, so headroom was 8000-3419 = 4,581 -- which .agents/research/2026-10-01-bug-hunt-e12-13.md:110 states verbatim ('against 4,581 free'). 4,543 is 4,581 - 38: the old header line's bytes subtracted a second time. A reader deriving the cap headroom from the plan gets a figure 38 short of the same project's research record.

findings.summary: Event-kind validation uses `in EVENT_KINDS` (also lines 678 and 757), which accepts prototype keys. The sibling checks at lines 691 and 793 use `Object.hasOwn`.
findings.failure_scenario: `window.until: constructor` (or `toString`, `__proto__`) passes `until in EVENT_KINDS`. The window then waits for an event kind that never occurs, so it is never closed by `until` and is silently counted as unclosed. `before: {on: toString}` and `any: [{on: constructor}]` are also accepted. The Object.hasOwn guard at 691 and 793 is the specification.

findings.summary: For `count` windows the noMatch/unclosed accounting is inverted relative to the documented contract. `closedBy` is never 'match' in count mode, so a `count` closed below at_least by `until` or `calls` is always added to `unclosed` and never to `noMatch`.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: {calls: 3, count: {...}, at_least: 2}` where fewer than 2 events match before the calls bound closes it. The doc at line 987 says this is decided with 'no match' and belongs in `noMatch`, but `unclosed` is incremented and `noMatch` stays 0. The reader is told the window was undecided when it was decided.

findings.summary: For `first` (and `count`) a window whose `until` is `session.end` is counted as `unclosed` when the stream ends, while the `absent` branch (line 1112) treats `until: session.end` as decided; `noMatch` is documented as decided by a bound, and the guarded sibling is the specification.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: {until: session.end, first: {on: file.changed}}` with no match before the stream ends increments `unclosed` (closedBy === 'session.end'), not `noMatch`, so the 'nothing matched before the bound' verdict is reported as 'log ended inside the window'. The same window written with `absent` is decided. The same holds for `count` below at_least at line 1104.

findings.summary: For `first`/`count` windows bounded by `until: session.end`, the branch order in `step()` always classifies the closing event as `'session.end'` rather than `'until'`, so a window that was actually decided by its declared bound is counted as `unclosed` instead of `noMatch`.
findings.failure_scenario: A stream-scoped handler declares `window: { until: session.end, count: {...}, at_least: 3 }` (legal: `calls`/`until: session.end` are only refused under `scope: session`, not `stream`). When the stream's `session.end` event arrives with `one.count < 3`, `step()` sets `closedBy = 'session.end'` at line 1172 because the `event.kind === 'session.end'` check is an `if` that runs before the `event.kind === window.until` check ever gets evaluated, even though `window.until` is itself `'session.end'`. `close()`'s count branch then does `if (closedBy === 'session.end') unclosed += 1; else noMatch += 1;` (line 1121ish), so this decided-by-its-own-bound window is reported via `unclosed` (documented as "the log ended inside this window", i.e. ambiguous/undecided) rather than `noMatch` (documented as "decided ... by a bound"). The `absent` mode has an explicit carve-out for this exact situation (`spec.until !== 'session.end'` check in `close()`), but `first` and `count` do not, so identical setups are classified inconsistently depending on window mode -- the guarded `absent` sibling is the specification the other two modes miss.

findings.summary: For count windows closed below `at_least`, the counters are swapped: closes by `until`/`calls` go to `unclosed`, and `noMatch` is only incremented for closedBy 'match', which never happens for count mode.
findings.failure_scenario: Take a count window with until: X that closes on X with count 0 < at_least 1. The result is noMatch 0, unclosed 1 instead of noMatch 1, unclosed 0. A session.end close is also counted wrongly. The test 'counts a count window closed below at_least' fails.

findings.summary: In count mode the unclosed/noMatch branches are inverted: a count window is never closed by 'match', so a window decided below at_least by until/calls is counted as unclosed, and one ended by session.end would count as noMatch if it ever were 'match'.
findings.failure_scenario: window: {until: session.end? no — until: agent.return, count: {on: tool.use.start}, at_least: 3}; the until event arrives after 1 match: the decided 'too few' verdict increments unclosed instead of noMatch, contradicting the noMatch doc; noMatch is always 0 for count handlers.

findings.summary: In stream scope, `session.end` closes a window before its own match is tried, and the compile-time clash check only covers an explicit `until`.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: {until: 'tool.use.end', first: {on: 'session.end'}}`, or an `absent`/`count` watcher on `session.end`, compiles. The `session.end` event closes the window as 'session.end' (`unclosed += 1`) and never reaches the match at line 1193. The result is no row and a wrong verdict. This is the same defect the clash refusal at line 719 exists to prevent.

findings.summary: On a case-insensitive filesystem (macOS default) two scheme names differing only in case share one directory and the tree then becomes unreadable, so the same committed repo reads on Linux and throws on macOS.

findings.summary: The `eq`/`ne` where-operators compare values with `===`, which is reference equality for the one array-typed event field (`argv`), so `{argv: {eq: [...]}}` type-checks but is silently always false (and `ne` always true).
findings.failure_scenario: A handler author writes `where: { argv: { eq: ["npm", "install"] } }` intending to match an exact command line. `pathType` reports argv's fieldType as 'array'; `operand()` on the literal `["npm","install"]` also reports type 'array', so the `right.type !== fieldType` guard passes and compilation succeeds silently. At runtime the compiled test does `value === right.get(trigger)`, comparing two distinct array objects, which is always false in JS -- so the condition can never be true for any event, exactly the 'operator on the wrong type... silently never true' class the file's own header comment names as the reason the loader is strict. Unlike gt/gte/lt/lte (require 'number'), contains/any_matches (require 'array' field + string arg) and matches (require 'string'), eq/ne has no type restriction that would catch or refuse this combination. No existing test exercises eq/ne against argv -- all argv where-tests in handler.test.ts use matches/contains/any_matches/followed_by/shares_token instead, confirming the gap is untested.

findings.summary: The `eq`/`ne`/`in` operators compare array-typed field values with `===`/`Set.has`, which is reference equality, so a literal array in a handler spec can never equal the event's own array.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with `on: command.run` and `where: { argv: { eq: ["git", "push"] } }` type-checks fine (`argv` is `array`, the literal `["git","push"]` is also typed `array`), but at runtime `value === right.get(trigger)` compares the event's `argv` array object against the literal array parsed from the spec -- two distinct array references that are never `===` even when their elements are identical. The condition is always false, so the handler silently matches nothing. The mirror case, `argv: { ne: [...] }`, is always true instead (any present array is `!==` the literal). `in: [[...], [...]]` over an array field has the same flaw via `Set.has`. This is exactly the "wrong handler runs green" class the file's own header (lines 10-15) says it exists to refuse -- but no refusal fires here because both sides are correctly typed `array`; only the equality semantics are wrong.

findings.summary: The clash check only compares `until` with the watched kind, but under scope: stream a `session.end` event closes every window before the match runs, so a window that watches `session.end` can never match either and is not refused.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: {calls: 5, first: {on: session.end}}` (or `until: tool.use.end` with `absent: {on: session.end}`) under the default stream scope: the accept loop sets closedBy='session.end' at line 1172 before `window.match` is reached, so `first` never emits and counts as `unclosed`, and `absent` emits its 'nothing matched' verdict about an event that did arrive. This is the same silent-zero class the `until` clash refusal above exists to prevent.

findings.summary: The clash refusal excludes `mode === 'first'`, although the comment says all three modes are refused. A `first` window whose `until` is the kind it watches can never match.
findings.failure_scenario: `until: agent.return` with `first: {on: agent.return}`. `until` is checked before the match, so the window closes with `noMatch` on the event it waits for and emits no rows. The comment cites this exact case as yielding rows [] and calls it a silent zero.

findings.summary: The doc says a `calls` window closes only once an event past the limit arrives and no call within the limit is unfinished, but `past` closes immediately and `running` is never consulted.
findings.failure_scenario: Calls 1 and 2 run in parallel, and call 2's result event (with a `file.changed`, say) arrives after an event with call 3 (past a `calls: 1` limit). The window has already closed as `calls`. The straggler is missed and a `first` or `absent` verdict is wrong.

findings.summary: The doc says a regex LONGER than MAX_REGEX_LENGTH is refused, but the check uses `>=`, so a pattern of exactly 300 characters is refused too.
findings.failure_scenario: A 300-character regex is refused with 'regex is 300 characters, over 300'.

findings.summary: The emit 'non-empty map' guard is `Object.keys(emitSpec).length < 0`, which is never true.
findings.failure_scenario: `{on: 'command.run', emit: {}}` is accepted and produces rows with empty `fields`, although the message says emit is required and non-empty.

findings.summary: The emit non-empty check `Object.keys(emitSpec).length < 0` is never true, so `emit: {}` compiles.
findings.failure_scenario: compileHandler({on:'command.run', emit:{}}) succeeds and emits rows with empty fields, instead of refusing with 'emit: is required, a non-empty map'.

findings.summary: The empty-list guard `spec.length < 0` can never be true, so `judged: []` is accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: compileHandler({..., judged: []}) returns a handler instead of throwing 'must be a non-empty list of names', so the test 'refuses an empty list' fails.

findings.summary: The envelope totals and the page ORDER BY assume a fixed-precision recorded_at, but the recorder's guard makes fractional seconds optional and text order puts '.500Z' before 'Z'.
findings.failure_scenario: Two recorded_at values equal to the second but differing in precision ('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z' and '2026-01-01T00:00:00.500Z') give an inverted envelope min/max and a non-chronological page walk. recorder.ts:208's regex makes the fraction optional and recorder.test.ts:480-494 asserts both forms are accepted.

findings.summary: The eq/ne and `in` type checks accept array operands for an array field, but the run-time comparison uses `===` / Set.has identity, so the condition can never be true (and `ne` is always true).
findings.failure_scenario: where: {argv: {in: [['ls','-la']]}} or where: {argv: {eq: ['ls']}} passes the typeOf check ('array' === 'array'), but an event's argv array is never the same object as the literal. The handler matches nothing and reports zero triggers with no error.

findings.summary: The eq/ne type check accepts a string literal against any field type (`right.type !== 'string'` short-circuit). `in` (line 412) and `gt`/`lt` (line 391) have similar gaps.
findings.failure_scenario: `seq: '5'` or `in: ['5']` on a number field passes compilation. `value === '5'` is never true for a number, so the condition is silently never true. Likewise `gt: '5'` compiles but the runtime `typeof bound === 'number'` check is never satisfied. A nonempty list matcher against an array field (line 363) compiles, but `===` compares by reference and never matches.

findings.summary: The eq/ne type check passes any string operand whatever the field type, so a string compared with a boolean or number field is accepted and never equal.
findings.failure_scenario: where: {is_error: 'yes'} compiles (the test expects 'is a string, the field is a boolean'); `false === 'yes'` is never true, so the handler silently matches nothing. `in` at line 412 has the same `|| 'string'` hole.

findings.summary: The filter check tests `filter.length === 0` rather than whether the filter exists in FILTERS, so an unknown filter is accepted and the render step silently skips it.
findings.failure_scenario: emit {x: '${head|upper}'} compiles and emits head unfiltered (for example 'bd' instead of an error), and the test expects /unknown filter upper/.

findings.summary: The filter check tests `filter.length === 0`, which is dead code because the regex requires `[a-z_]+`; unknown filter names are never refused.
findings.failure_scenario: '${command|basenme}' compiles and renders unfiltered; '${command|constructor}' resolves FILTERS['constructor'] to Object and emits a String wrapper object.

findings.summary: The gt/gte/lt/lte check validates only the field type, not the operand's type, so a non-numeric bound is accepted and the comparison is silently always false.
findings.failure_scenario: where: {hits: {gt: '0'}} on search.run compiles; at runtime `typeof bound === 'number'` is false, so no event ever matches.

findings.summary: The handler hash is `sha256Hex(JSON.stringify(parsed))`, not the imported (and unused) `canonicalJson`, so key order changes the identity, contrary to the stated 'canonical parsed form' contract.
findings.failure_scenario: The same handler with keys written in a different order ({emit, where, on} vs {on, where, emit}) gets different hashes, so reformatted YAML looks like a new handler. The test 'ignores key order' fails.

findings.summary: The handler hash is computed with JSON.stringify(parsed) rather than the imported canonicalJson, so key order (formatting) changes the identity, contradicting the module's stated identity contract.
findings.failure_scenario: Two YAML files with identical meaning but keys `on` and `emit` in different order produce different `hash` values, so the same handler is treated as two distinct handlers.

findings.summary: The handler's shipped header asserts the review.finding event cannot carry reviewer_model, but the event declares it and the normalizer emits it; the handler's own emit block drops the field.
findings.failure_scenario: A maintainer reads the header, believes replay-side stratification by reviewer model is impossible, and does not add the field. event.ts:167 declares reviewer_model on the kind, normalize.ts:409 emits it, and EVENT_DERIVE_VERSION is 11. The header comment dates 2026-09-26; the field landed 2026-09-28 and the bead it awaited has shipped.

findings.summary: The hash uses `JSON.stringify(parsed)`, which depends on key order, while the header says identity is the hash of the canonical form. `canonicalJson` is imported but never used.
findings.failure_scenario: Two YAML files with the same handler but keys written in a different order (`on` then `emit` vs `emit` then `on`) get different `hash` values, so they look like different definitions. Non-finite numbers and `undefined` are also not canonicalized.

findings.summary: The headroom figure is quoted on one measurement base where the figure it is compared against uses the other, and neither names which object it counts.
findings.failure_scenario: E12.13's '4,619 free' is 8000-3,381 (the asc doctor count); E12.14's '4,555 free' is 8000-3,445 (the stdout count). Under the first definition the current figure is 4,556; under the second the earlier one is 4,618. findings.summary: The hook script is written via renameSync with no symlink resolution, while settings.json written four lines earlier IS resolved — the rename replaces a symlink instead of its target.
findings.failure_scenario: A repo keeps .claude/ascend-hook.sh symlinked into a shared dotfiles repo. isScriptCurrent reads through the link, finds different content, and writeAtomically renames the temp file onto the link path — destroying the link, leaving a stale shared target, and breaking every other checkout. findings.summary: The identity hash is taken over the raw parsed form, not a normalized one, so spelling out a default changes the hash even though the meaning is the same.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with `scope: stream`, capture `group: 1`, or each `from: 0` hashes differently from the same handler with those keys omitted, although both compile to identical behaviour. findings.summary: The identity hash uses `JSON.stringify(parsed)`, not the canonical form the header says it uses (`canonicalJson` is imported but unused). Key order therefore changes the hash.
findings.failure_scenario: Two YAML handlers with identical meaning but keys in a different order (`on` before `where` versus `where` before `on`) get different `hash` values. This contradicts 'IDENTITY is the sha256 of the canonical parsed form: formatting does not change it'. It also gives spurious identity changes, and two handler versions can be treated as different.

findings.summary: The in-flight check uses `call < limit`, so a running call exactly at the limit does not hold the window open.
findings.failure_scenario: Trigger call 1 with calls: 1 (limit 2). Call 2 is started but not ended when call 3 arrives. The window closes immediately with 'calls', losing call 2's later event, contrary to 'no call within the limit is still unfinished'.

findings.summary: The issued dedupe set spans all types while store ids are namespaced per type, so two different types emitting the same raw key mint a meaningless '#2' and over-count keyCollisions.
findings.failure_scenario: A denied Bash check makes tool_denial emit 'sess-1:t1', then verification_run for the same tool_use id is suffixed 'sess-1:t1#2'. keyCollisions increments and the warning claims an event key repeated within a transcript, which is false for a cross-type pair; the meaningless suffix is baked into a stored id.

findings.summary: The judged-vs-emit conflict check has `&& index === 0`, so only the first judged name is checked against `emit`.
findings.failure_scenario: `judged: [a, b]` with `emit: {b: ...}`. `b` is at index 1, so the check is skipped. The row then both emits `b` and declares it judged, which the doc comment says must be refused at load.

findings.summary: The judged-vs-emitted conflict is only checked for `index === 0`, so any later judged name that is also emitted is accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: `judged: [a, b]` with `emit: {b: '${path}'}` loads cleanly. The row asserts a value for `b` and also declares it judged, which the function's own doc says must be refused.

findings.summary: The justification for keeping the note out of RECORD_COMMAND cites an example consumer that does not exist.
findings.failure_scenario: The doc argues a consumer wanting the bare command -- naming 'the script's resolution comment, a test asserting the spelling' -- would otherwise have to parse the note back off the end. Grep receipt: `grep -rn "RECORD_COMMAND" packages/ --include=*.ts` returns exactly two source consumers, brief-text.ts:142 and install-hook.ts:289, and both interpolate the note; the script's resolution comment (.claude/ascend-hook.sh:24-25) names no command. findings.failure_scenario: calls: 1 with the trigger on call 1: limit=1, so a command.run on call 2 counts as past and the window closes with count 0; the 'holds a calls window open' and 'first: emits at the match' tests return [].

findings.summary: The limit is stored as `event.call + window.calls - 1` and then compared with `event.call >= limit` (line 1165), so a `calls: N` window stops about two calls earlier than the documented `trigger.call + N`.
findings.failure_scenario: searchMiss (calls: 2) with a trigger at call 1 and a correcting search at call 2: limit=2 and past=true, so the window closes by 'calls' before the match is checked. No row is emitted where the test expects one.

findings.summary: The line this change adds to make recording reachable — `Record with: asc record TYPE --json -` — names a command that reads its document from standard input, which the payload neither supplies nor mentions; run verbatim it exits 1 with `standard input is not valid JSON: Unexpected end of JSON input.`, and ARCHITECTURE.md:333 states the same spelling with the `(stdin)` qualifier that this rendering drops.
findings.failure_scenario: A session at SessionStart reads `Record with: asc record TYPE --json -`, substitutes a type name, and runs it — the exact behaviour the fix exists to enable. It gets a JSON parse error about a document it never intended to write, and the payload gives it neither the type's properties nor a pointer to `asc record --help`, so recovering costs two more steps (`asc types show`, then `--prop` or a hand-written object) in a payload whose purpose is to remove steps. Measured in a scratch project: `node …/bin.js record review_completed --json - < /dev/null` → exit 1 with the error above; the standalone alternative `asc record decision --prop chosen=alpha --prop rationale=testing` → exit 0.

findings.summary: The mode-vs-flag gate covers only --temporal, --blocks and --permutations; the other eight mode-specific flags are silently accepted and ignored by modes that cannot use them.
findings.failure_scenario: asc stats decision --assoc --threshold abc exits 0 with a full table and no diagnostic, while asc stats decision --cluster --threshold abc exits 2. A caller switching modes keeps a flag they believe is applied; worse, the value is never parsed, so an input the tool refuses in the owning mode is accepted silently elsewhere.

findings.summary: The nested-path guard is `rest.length > 1`, so a path with one extra segment after the index (e.g. `argv.1.x`) is typed as a string.
findings.failure_scenario: where {'argv.1.x': 'foo'} compiles, but read() returns undefined for a string element, so the condition is silently never true.

findings.summary: The non-empty check for `in` is `arg.length < 0`, which is never true. Empty `in: []` is accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: `head: { in: [] }` compiles and never matches, a silent never-true condition that the compiler is meant to refuse (`not: {in: []}` is always true).

findings.summary: The open window stores the raw trigger `scope` instead of `emitScope`, contrary to the adjacent comment, so ${before.…} fields are always absent on rows emitted by windowed handlers.
findings.failure_scenario: Handler with before: {on: tool.use.start} and a window first:; emit x: '${before.command}'. A prior matching event exists, yet the row emitted at the window match has x = '' because the raw scope reads 'before.command' off the trigger (undefined).

findings.summary: The record now carries two unreconciled byte counts for the same object, 221 bytes apart, and the amendment did not name the difference.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader compares the body's '3,603 bytes stdout' (line 78, measured 2026-09-28) against the amended Status cell's '3,381 -> 3,444 as asc doctor counts it' and cannot tell which registry each describes, because the cell attributes the whole difference to the fix while 222 bytes of it are a registry change. findings.summary: The recovery the validation error offers is refused by the command the brief advertises, so the 'failure that teaches the next step' the E12.14 decision rests on is a dead end.
findings.failure_scenario: A session pipes `{}` to the advertised `asc record TYPE --json -` and is told `Supply the value with --prop=chosen=<value>`. Applied to the form it was reached from, that yields exit 2: `a document (-) and entry flags (--prop/--na/--evidence) cannot be combined: they describe the same entry twice.` (record.ts:524-533, measured). IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md:2478-2480 records this exact recovery as the criterion for choosing stdin over the flag form: 'the criterion is which failure teaches the next step: piping {} yields --prop=chosen=<value>'.

findings.summary: The refusal of `until: session.end` under `scope: session` also requires `calls !== undefined`, so the plain shape is accepted, and at run time the first stream's session.end matches `window.until` and closes every window in the session.
findings.failure_scenario: {scope: session, on: file.changed, window: {until: session.end, first: {on: check.run}}} compiles (the test expects /session.end is one event per STREAM/). At run time a subagent's session.end closes main's windows with 'until' and counts noMatch.

findings.summary: The regex length check uses `>=` against MAX_REGEX_LENGTH, but the documented rule is that source 'longer than' the max is refused.
findings.failure_scenario: A regex of exactly 300 characters is refused with 'regex is 300 characters, over 300'.

findings.summary: The regex length check uses `>=`, so a 300-character source is refused although the documented rule is 'longer than' 300. The error message then says '300 characters, over 300'.
findings.failure_scenario: A 300-char pattern throws 'regex is 300 characters, over 300'.

findings.summary: The row builder converts an undefined template result to '' so the single-reference template's deliberate 'omit when absent' behavior is lost and absent is indistinguishable from empty.
findings.failure_scenario: emit: {path: '${before.file_path}'} on a trigger with no before match: the template returns undefined as designed but the row has fields.path === '' instead of no path field.

findings.summary: The running set adds `event.call` on tool.use.start but deletes `event.seq` on tool.use.end, so finished calls are never removed, or unrelated calls are.
findings.failure_scenario: tool.use.start call 2 (seq 1), then tool.use.end call 2 (seq 5): delete(5) leaves 2 in the set forever, so any straggler logic that read `running` would hold windows open indefinitely.

findings.summary: The running-call tracking is inconsistent and unused. `tool.use.start` adds `event.call`, but `tool.use.end` deletes `event.seq`. The `running` set is never consulted when closing, although the doc (lines 1018-1020) promises a window closes only when no call within the limit is unfinished.
findings.failure_scenario: Parallel calls finish out of order. The first event past the limit closes the window at line 1165 with `past`, even though a call within the limit has not ended. Its later match is lost, so a `first` or `count` verdict is wrong or an `absent` verdict is a false positive. The delete of seq never removes the added call number.

findings.summary: The same measurement is cited as 3,381 bytes in `brief-text.ts:92`, dogfood/0028 and IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md:2357, and as 3,382 bytes in `commands/types/brief.ts:12`, `test/init.test.ts:570` and `test/install-hook.test.ts:442`; IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md:2360 records the off-by-one as corrected, but the correction reached one of the four sites.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader comparing the source comment to the test comment cannot tell which value is meant, and the next person to re-measure has no way to know which object they are correcting. Both numbers are right for different objects and no site names its object: measured on this repository, `asc types brief | wc -c` is 3420 (stdout, including `this.log`'s trailing newline → 3,382 pre-change) while the doctor's count, which excludes it, is 3419 (→ 3,381 pre-change).

findings.summary: The same-stream ordering guard is `event.seq >= one.trigger.seq`, while the documented rule is `seq > trigger.seq`, so an event with the same seq as the trigger counts as 'after'.
findings.failure_scenario: A duplicate or re-offered event with the trigger's seq (for example, a replay that offers the trigger twice) matches its own window and emits a 'first' row, or increments count, from the trigger itself.

findings.summary: The sentence reconciling F3's 'one measurement, two objects' pairs a line+newline cost against a line-only cost, so it is itself one quantity measured two ways.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader re-deriving the budget computes 4,619 - 62 = 4,557 free and expects a 3,443-byte digest, but `asc doctor` reports 3,444 (measured). The published values are 38 = 37+1 (old line including its newline) and 62 (new line excluding it); the consistent pairs are 37 -> 62 or 38 -> 63, and the command charges 63 -- brief.ts:183 is `Buffer.byteLength(`${RECORD_COMMAND_LINE}\n`)`. Three independent passes reproduced this.

findings.summary: The session-scope `calls` refusal checks `typeof calls !== 'number'`, which can never be true because a non-number was already refused at line 587, so session-scoped windows with a numeric `calls` are accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: {scope: session, window: {calls: 2, until: prompt.submit, first: ...}} compiles, and calls from different streams collide, closing windows on unrelated streams. {scope: session, window: {calls: 2, first: ...}} is refused with the 'needs until' message instead of 'cannot count calls'.

findings.summary: The session-scope `calls` refusal checks `typeof calls !== 'number'`, which can never be true here because a non-number was already refused at line 587, so session-scoped windows with a numeric `calls` are accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: {scope: session, window: {calls: 2, until: prompt.submit, first: ...}} compiles, and calls from different streams collide, closing windows on unrelated streams. {scope: session, window: {calls: 2, first: ...}} is refused with the 'needs until' message instead of 'cannot count calls'.

findings.summary: The session-scope `calls` refusal tests `calls !== undefined && typeof calls !== 'number'`. Line 586 already guarantees `calls` is a number or undefined, so the check is dead and `calls` is never refused under session scope.
findings.failure_scenario: The handler `scope: session, window: {calls: 5, until: 'agent.return', first: {...}}` compiles. `call` numbers collide across streams, so the window closes early, late, or never. The intended refusal message is unreachable. The check should be `calls !== undefined`.

findings.summary: The session-scope refusal of `calls` only fires when `typeof calls !== 'number'`, which the earlier check already rejects. A numeric `calls` under `scope: session` is therefore accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: `scope: session, window: {calls: 3, until: agent.return, ...}` compiles. The limit then compares call numbers from different streams, so the window closes early, late, or never: exactly the case the comment says is refused.

findings.summary: The session-scope refusal of `calls` tests `typeof calls !== 'number'`. A valid numeric `calls` (the only value that reaches here) is therefore never refused, and the error message describes a check that cannot fire.
findings.failure_scenario: `scope: session, window: {calls: 5, until: agent.return, first: {...}}` compiles. The `calls` limit then compares `event.call` numbers across streams, and windows close early, late or never. The condition should be `calls !== undefined`.

findings.summary: The single-form window match calls only the compiled where and never checks event.kind === kind, despite the comment stating the kind check belongs to the match.
findings.failure_scenario: window: {calls: 3, first: {on: tool.use.end}} with no where (compileWhere returns ()=>true): the very next event of any kind (e.g. a tool.use.start or message) after the trigger matches and emits the row with window.first.* read from the wrong event.

findings.summary: The single-kind window's `match` never checks `event.kind === kind`, even though the comment above says the kind check belongs to the match; the any-form (line 688) does check it.
findings.failure_scenario: Take `first: {on: check.run}` with a where over envelope fields (e.g. ts) or with no where. An earlier tool.use.start that satisfies the where is taken as the match, so window.first.* reads the wrong event ('early' instead of 'late'). The test 'first: the window kind is part of the match' fails.

findings.summary: The slice start index is `xs.length - n - 1`, which is one too low, so `lastN` returns n+1 elements instead of n.
findings.failure_scenario: lastN([1,2,3,4,5], 2) evaluates slice(2) and returns [3,4,5] instead of [4,5]. lastN([1,2,3], 0) evaluates slice(2) and returns [3] instead of []. lastN([1,2,3], 3) evaluates slice(-1) and returns [3] instead of [1,2,3], because the negative index wraps around.

findings.summary: The straggler check `call <= limit` counts every running call up to the limit, including calls that started BEFORE the trigger and so are not inside the window; the intended range is [trigger.call, limit].
findings.failure_scenario: Trigger at call 7 with `calls: 2` (limit 9) while an earlier call 3 (for example an async spawn or an interrupted tool with no tool.use.end) is still in `running`: events with call > 9 arrive but call 3 satisfies `call <= 9`, so the window is held open. An `absent` verdict is never emitted and the window is counted `unclosed` at stream end (or its close is delayed). Windows are keyed off unrelated calls.

findings.summary: The straggler check `call <= limit` includes calls started before the trigger (call < trigger.call), not just calls within (trigger.call, limit].
findings.failure_scenario: An earlier call 2 is still running (no `tool.use.end`) when a trigger at call 5 with `calls: 1` opens. An event at call 7 is past the limit of 6 but `running` still holds 2 (2 <= 6), so the window stays open, absorbing unrelated events with call <= limit and possibly never closing by calls.

findings.summary: The straggler check `call <= limit` includes calls started before the trigger, not only calls in [trigger.call, limit].
findings.failure_scenario: A long-running call 2 is still in `running` when a trigger at call 5 opens a `calls: 3` window (limit 8). Events past call 8 never close the window because call 2 is `<= 8`, so it stays open until `until` or session.end. It is then reported as unclosed or matched against events far outside the intended window.

findings.summary: The straggler check `call <= limit` includes calls that started before the trigger, so an unrelated earlier call that never ends holds the window open.
findings.failure_scenario: A `tool.use.start` for call 2 with no matching end (an orphan or dropped end event). A `calls: 3` window triggered at call 10 has limit 13. The running set still contains 2 (<= 13), so the window never closes by `calls` until `session.end`, and `noMatch` and its rows are delayed or turn into unclosed.

findings.summary: The straggler check uses `call < limit`, but a running call equal to the limit is still inside the window (`call` at most trigger.call + N).
findings.failure_scenario: With the window's last call still running (call == limit) when an event past the limit arrives, the window closes as 'calls' before that call's late event is counted or matched.

findings.summary: The subject is sliced to `MAX_SUBJECT_LENGTH - 1` characters, one fewer than the documented cap (the capture path at line 1234 repeats this).

findings.summary: The subject truncation slices to `MAX_SUBJECT_LENGTH - 1`, so a regex sees 99,999 characters, not the documented 100,000. The capture path at line 1234 repeats it.
findings.failure_scenario: A pattern anchored on the 100,000th character (e.g. `x$` on a 100,000-character string ending in x) fails to match.

findings.summary: The template reference regex only accepts a single lowercase `[a-z_]+` filter, so `${x|Basename}` or `${x|snake|basename}` is not matched as a reference and is silently emitted as literal text, with no unknown-filter refusal.
findings.failure_scenario: emit: `path: "${file_path|Basename}"` (or two chained filters) compiles without error because the regex skips the reference. Every row then carries the literal string `${file_path|Basename}` as the value. This is the silent wrong-result-that-runs-green class the file says it refuses everywhere else.

findings.summary: The template reference regex only accepts filter names matching `[a-z_]+`, so a reference whose filter has uppercase letters, digits, or spaces does not match at all, bypassing both the unknown-filter and field-name refusals.
