findings.summary: The test named 'derives the head count by reading the tail file once, not by recounting per append' does not test the 'once', so the O(1) rollover claim the module's header argues for at length has no guard.
findings.failure_scenario: Deleting the `heads` cache and calling `inspect(segments)` on every `append` — making the writer O(n^2), the exact shape the module doc says it exists to prevent — leaves the suite at 26 passed / 26. The test only asserts that a re-opened writer continues from disk, which a recounting implementation also does. No test counts `readFileSync`/`statSync` calls.

findings.summary: The test named 'reads files in numeric order, so 0002 follows 0001 and not the reverse' never inspects read order, so reversing file order leaves the entire suite green — a false green over the property the module calls load-bearing.
findings.failure_scenario: Mutating `recordFilesIn`'s sort from `(a, b) => a.index - b.index` to `(a, b) => b.index - a.index` leaves the suite at 26 passed / 26. Independently reproduced by the main session, with the mutation reverted and the file hash verified afterward. The test asserts only `writer.written` (the writer's own order) and `toHaveLength(2)`. This matters because the module's ORDER section states that file order IS meaning for type and scheme lines — it defines version numbers — so a regression here silently renumbers versions while the suite reports green.

findings.summary: The test-local `const RECORD_COMMAND = 'Record with: asc record TYPE --json -'` holds `RECORD_COMMAND_LINE`'s value under `RECORD_COMMAND`'s name, while the source exports `RECORD_COMMAND = 'asc record TYPE --json -'` and gives the longer string the name `RECORD_COMMAND_LINE` — so the identifier this change exists to unify holds two different values in two artifacts.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader greps `RECORD_COMMAND` to find the one spelling and gets two definitions holding two different strings, with nothing saying which is the command and which is the sentence — the confusion the constant was introduced to end. Hardcoding rather than importing is correct (an imported constant cannot fail), but the name is free; `test/install-hook.test.ts` already uses a neutral `const command = …` for the same purpose.

findings.summary: The token regex is `{5,}` but the documented minimum (and test comments) is 4 characters, so 4-character tokens never count toward shares_token.
findings.failure_scenario: shares_token between pattern 'yaml' and path 'config.yaml' finds no overlap because 'yaml' is not a token, so the window never matches and the handler reports the path as unused.

findings.summary: The unknown-filter check is dead: the regex `[a-z_]+` guarantees a non-empty filter, so `filter.length === 0` never holds. Unknown filter names are never validated against `FILTERS`.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: {x: '${path|basenmae}'}` compiles. At render time `FILTERS['basenmae']` is undefined, so the raw unfiltered text is emitted. A filter with uppercase or digits, such as `${path|Base}`, does not match the reference regex at all and is emitted as literal text.

findings.summary: The unknown-filter check tests `filter.length === 0`, which is impossible for the `[a-z_]+` capture, so unknown filters are never refused.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: {f: '${path|basname}'}` compiles. At render, `FILTERS['basname']` is undefined and the raw unfiltered path is emitted. `|Basename` does not match the reference regex at all, so the whole `${...}` is emitted literally. `|constructor` or `|__proto__` resolve to Object.prototype members because FILTERS is looked up without `hasOwn`.

findings.summary: The unknown-key check lets a top-level `window.where` through even though it is never read.
findings.failure_scenario: window: {until: x, where: {...}, first: {on: y}} compiles and the where filter is silently dropped, so the window matches more events than the author wrote.

findings.summary: The until/watched-kind clash check skips `mode === 'first'`, so a `first` window whose `until` equals its watched kind is accepted even though it can never be decided.
findings.failure_scenario: window: {until: 'agent.return', first: {on: 'agent.return'}} compiles; at runtime every agent.return closes the window via `until` before the match runs. It yields rows [] and counts a noMatch, which is the silent-zero case the comment says is refused.

findings.summary: The until/watched-kind clash is refused only when mode is not 'first', but the comment says all three modes are dead-ends; a first-window is closed by its own until before it can match.
findings.failure_scenario: until: agent.return with first: {on: agent.return} compiles; every window closes on 'until' and counts as noMatch, so the handler never emits a row.

findings.summary: The window call limit is computed as `event.call + calls - 1`, but the documented and tested semantics are `trigger.call + N` (calls within N after the trigger).
findings.failure_scenario: With `calls: 2` and a trigger at call 1, limit is 2. A matching event at call 2 counts as past the limit and is ignored, so the 'first: emits at the match' test yields no row. With `calls: 1`, the trigger's own later same-call events close the window at once.

findings.summary: The window guard uses `event.seq >= one.trigger.seq`. The comment says events must be after the trigger, that is strictly greater.
findings.failure_scenario: If an event other than the trigger shares the trigger's seq in a stream, it is counted as inside the window although it is not later than the trigger.

findings.summary: The window limit is `event.seq + window.calls`, but it is compared against `event.call` (line 1165), and seq and call are unrelated counters.
findings.failure_scenario: The trigger is command.run at seq 3, call 1, with calls: 1. The limit becomes 4 instead of 2, so later events with call 3 or 4 are still counted inside the window. In a long stream, seq can far exceed call, so the window never closes by calls.

findings.summary: The window limit is computed as `event.seq + window.calls`, but it is compared against `event.call` at line 1165. The doc at line 1017 says the limit is `trigger.call + N`.
findings.failure_scenario: A trigger has seq 100 and call 3, with `calls: 2`. The limit is 102, but calls are small numbers. The window stays open for about 99 extra calls, or closes at the wrong point, and the `first`, `count` and `absent` verdicts are wrong. seq and call are different counters.

findings.summary: The window limit is set to `event.seq + window.calls`, but it is compared against `event.call` and documented as `trigger.call + N`.
findings.failure_scenario: Trigger at seq 200, call 5, with calls:2. The limit becomes 202, so the window stays open across dozens of calls (call 6..202) instead of closing after call 7, and it matches events far outside the window.

findings.summary: The window stores the raw `scope` instead of `emitScope`, contrary to the comment above it, so `${before.*}` is lost on every windowed handler's rows.
findings.failure_scenario: Handler with `before: {on: file.read}`, `window: {calls: 3, first: {...}}` and `emit: {prev: '${before.path}'}`. `unsatisfiedBefore` is not incremented (a match was found), but on the window row `one.scope('before.path')` resolves to `read(event, 'before.path')`, which is undefined. The field comes out empty even though a reference exists.

findings.summary: The window's stored `scope` is the raw trigger scope, not the `before`-wrapped `emitScope`, although the comment says the wrapped scope is stored. `${before.x}` therefore resolves to nothing on every windowed row.
findings.failure_scenario: Handler with `before: {on: file.read}`, a `window`, and `emit: {prev: ${before.path}}`. The trigger finds an earlier file.read, but the row is built later from `one.scope`, which is the raw scope. It calls `read(event, 'before.path')` on the trigger and returns undefined, so `prev` is emitted as ''. `unsatisfiedBefore` is not incremented, so the loss is invisible.

findings.summary: Under scope: stream, session.end always closes open windows before the match check runs, so a window that watches `session.end` can never match. The until/watched clash guard at line 719 refuses exactly this shape, but it does not cover session.end.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: {calls: 5, first: {on: session.end}}` with the default stream scope compiles. When the stream's session.end arrives, line 1172 sets closedBy='session.end' and the window is counted as unclosed. It never emits a row, so the handler looks green over a signal it can never see. Same for `count: {on: session.end}` (never reaches at_least) and `absent: {on: session.end}`.

findings.summary: When `before:` finds no earlier match, the code does `unsatisfiedBefore += 0`, so the counter never goes above 0.
findings.failure_scenario: A check.run trigger with before: {on: file.changed} and no earlier file.changed emits a row with no `prior` field, and unsatisfiedBefore stays 0 (expected 1). The unsatisfiable join is never reported.

findings.summary: When `each.field` is absent or not an array, or `from` is past its end, or no item matches, rows() returns [] and no counter records it. The trigger (or a decided window) disappears silently.
findings.failure_scenario: each: {field: argv, from: 5} on a command.run whose argv has 2 items: triggers is incremented but no row, noMatch or unclosed is produced. A first-window match with that trigger is consumed with no output, so triggers - rows cannot be reconciled.

findings.summary: When `each.field` is absent/not an array, or every item is filtered by `from`/`matches`, `rows()` returns [] and nothing is counted, so a counted trigger vanishes without being unclosed/noMatch.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with `each: {field: argv, from: 5, as: x}` on events whose argv has 3 items: `triggers` increments but zero rows are emitted and no counter explains the gap.

findings.summary: When a `before:` reference finds no earlier match, `unsatisfiedBefore += 0` never counts it.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with `before:` where the trigger has no earlier matching event in its partition. The `${before.…}` fields are absent, but `unsatisfiedBefore` stays 0. This is the counter the doc comment says exists so unsatisfied references are never silent. It should be `+= 1`.

findings.summary: When a `before:` reference finds no earlier match, `unsatisfiedBefore` is incremented by 0, so the counter never moves.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with `before:` whose first trigger has no earlier matching event: `run.unsatisfiedBefore` stays 0 although the row's `${before.*}` fields are absent. The documented 'reported verdict' is always 0, so unsatisfiable joins look like a handler with nothing to join.

findings.summary: When a handler has no window, the trigger path calls `row(...)` directly instead of `rows(...)`, so `each` is ignored; the window paths (lines 1103, 1197) do go through `rows`.
findings.failure_scenario: Take a handler with `each: {field: argv, from: 2, matches: '^[a-z]+-\d+$', as: bead}` and no window, over argv ['bd','close','a-1','--x','b-2']. It emits one row with stage '' instead of two rows (a-1, b-2). The test 'fans out one row per matching array element' fails.

findings.summary: When a stream-scoped window has `until: session.end`, the close is tagged 'session.end' instead of 'until'. Only `absent` mode treats that as a decision; `first` and `count` count it as `unclosed` instead of `noMatch`, and count rows carry closed_by 'session.end'.
findings.failure_scenario: window: {until: session.end, first: {on: tool.use.start}} with no tool call before the stream ends: the window has reached its declared bound, so it should count as noMatch, but close() increments unclosed. The compile error at line 724 even recommends session.end 'to let the stream end decide it'. This is inconsistent with the absent-mode guard at line 1112.

findings.summary: When n exceeds xs.length, the start index goes negative and slice counts from the end of the array, so the result is wrong instead of the whole array. Fixing the off-by-one alone does not resolve this.
findings.failure_scenario: With the off-by-one fixed to `slice(xs.length - n)`, lastN([1,2,3], 4) evaluates slice(-1) and returns [3] instead of [1,2,3]. Clamping the start, for example `xs.slice(Math.max(0, xs.length - n))`, handles this case. Negative n is also unvalidated.

findings.summary: When no earlier `before:` match exists the code does `unsatisfiedBefore += 0`, so the counter stays at 0 forever.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with before: {on: tool.use.start} whose trigger arrives first in the stream emits a row with no before.* fields, and unsatisfiedBefore reports 0 instead of 1 (the test at handler.test.ts:1068 expects 1).

findings.summary: When the `each` array field is absent on the trigger, `rows` emits one row with the `each.as` variable unresolved instead of zero rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A bd close handler with each: {field:'argv', as:'bead'} and a trigger without argv emits one row where `stage` is missing, rather than no rows.

findings.summary: When the `each` field is absent on the trigger, `rows()` returns [] silently: the trigger is already counted in `triggers`, yet no row, noMatch or other counter records the loss.
findings.failure_scenario: `each: {field: argv, as: arg}` on a command.run event whose transcript did not carry `argv`: `triggers` is incremented but zero rows are emitted, so `triggers` exceeds rows with no counter accounting for the difference, which reads like a handler that forgot to match.

findings.summary: When the handler's own trigger kind is `session.end`, the stream's windows are deleted at line 1223 before the trigger is pushed, so the new window opens after the stream's teardown and can never be closed.
findings.failure_scenario: `on: session.end` with a `window`: the window is added to `open` after `open.delete(key)`. No later event of that stream closes it, so it sits in `open` (memory retained) until `finish()`, where it is counted `unclosed` although it was decided at stream end, and its rows are never emitted.

findings.summary: With `each`, a trigger (or decided window) whose list field is missing/non-array or whose items all fail `each.matches` produces zero rows while triggers is incremented and neither noMatch nor unclosed is, reintroducing the unaccounted-trigger silence.
findings.failure_scenario: Handler with `each: {field: argv, from: 2, matches: '^asc-'}` on command.run with argv ['bd','close'] → triggers=1, rows=0, unclosed=0, noMatch=0; a `first` window matched with such a trigger likewise vanishes.

findings.summary: `Object.keys(emitSpec).length < 0` is never true, so `emit: {}` is accepted although the message says 'a non-empty map'.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with `emit: {}` compiles and produces rows with empty `fields`.

findings.summary: `Object.keys(emitSpec).length < 0` is never true, so an empty `emit` map compiles despite the 'non-empty map' requirement.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: {}` compiles and every trigger emits a row with no fields, which is the silent-empty handler this file sets out to refuse.

findings.summary: `WINDOW_KEYS` contains `any`, which is only valid inside first/count/absent. A top-level `window.any` passes the strict key check and is then silently ignored.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: {calls: 3, first: {on: file.read}, any: [{on: file.changed}]}` compiles and never watches `file.changed`. That is the silently-never-true handler the file claims to refuse.

findings.summary: `accept` calls `record(event)` before `step(event)`, although `record` is documented as running AFTER the trigger body so that `before` means strictly earlier.
findings.failure_scenario: For `on: file.changed` with `before: {on: file.changed}`, the trigger is recorded first and `lastBefore.get(key)` returns the trigger itself. `${before.path}` equals the trigger's own path, and `unsatisfiedBefore` is never incremented, even for the first event in the stream.

findings.summary: `accept` calls `record(event)` before `step(event)`, although `record` is documented to run after the trigger body so that `before` means strictly earlier. A trigger that also matches `before` becomes its own reference.
findings.failure_scenario: `on: tool.use.start` with `before: {on: tool.use.start}`: each trigger's `${before.*}` reads its own fields instead of the previous start event's, and `unsatisfiedBefore` is never incremented for the first trigger.

findings.summary: `accept` calls `record(event)` before `step(event)`, but the docs (lines 1243-1244, 1270-1274) say recording happens AFTER the trigger body. When the trigger kind equals `before.on` and matches, the trigger becomes its own `before` reference.
findings.failure_scenario: The handler is `on: tool.use.start` with `before: {on: tool.use.start}`. The event is recorded into `lastBefore` first, so `earlier` is the trigger itself and `unsatisfiedBefore` is never incremented for the first trigger. `${before.x}` returns the trigger's own field instead of the previous match.

findings.summary: `accept` calls `record(event)` before `step(event)`, so a trigger whose kind is also the `before.on` kind stores itself first and then reads itself as 'the most recent earlier match'.
findings.failure_scenario: {on: file.changed, before: {on: file.changed}} with a single file.changed path=/self.ts gives prior='/self.ts' and unsatisfiedBefore=0. The test expects prior to be absent and unsatisfiedBefore=1.

findings.summary: `any`/`all` are refused when `matcher.length <= 1`, although the message says 'non-empty list'. A one-element list is valid, and the sibling check for window `any` uses `=== 0`.
findings.failure_scenario: `where: { any: [{ head: 'bd' }] }` is refused as 'must be a non-empty list'. An empty list is also refused, but for the wrong reason.

findings.summary: `any`/`all` lists are refused when `matcher.length <= 1`, while the message says 'non-empty'.
findings.failure_scenario: `where: {any: [{head: 'bd'}]}` is refused with 'must be a non-empty list' although it is a valid single-element list. Compare the window `any` guard at line 668, which uses `length === 0`.

findings.summary: `arg.length < 0` is never true, so `in: []` compiles into a condition that can never be true.
findings.failure_scenario: where `{head: {in: []}}` compiles and matches nothing, silently, instead of being refused with 'in needs a non-empty list'.

findings.summary: `at_least` is checked only for `typeof number` and `< 1`, although the message says 'whole number'. Fractions, NaN and Infinity pass. The sibling `calls` check (586) uses `Number.isInteger`.
findings.failure_scenario: `at_least: .nan` (YAML) or `Infinity`: `atLeast < 1` is false, so it is accepted, and `count >= NaN` is never true, so the window never emits. `at_least: 1.5` behaves as 2.

findings.summary: `before:` is refused under `scope: session` only when `kind === 'session.end'`. The message and the comment at line 1037 say it is refused under session scope entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: The handler `scope: session, before: {on: tool.use.start}` compiles. `lastBefore` is keyed by session, so its 'most recent match' depends on the file read order. That is the cross-stream ordering verdict the refusal was meant to prevent.

findings.summary: `before:` under `scope: session` is refused only when `before.on === 'session.end'`, so every other before kind is accepted under session scope, where the order is file order.
findings.failure_scenario: {scope: session, on: check.run, before: {on: file.changed}} compiles; the test expects /before: is not available under scope: session/. The reference then depends on which transcript file was read first.

findings.summary: `calls` (line 586) and `at_least` (line 654) are validated with `< 0`, although the messages say 'at least 1'. `calls: 0` is accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: `window: { calls: 0, first: ... }` compiles, and the limit falls before the trigger's own call. The window closes at once with a noMatch and never sees an event. `at_least: 0` compiles too and means the same as the default.

findings.summary: `canonicalJson(parsed)` throws a TypeError for non-finite numbers, not a HandlerError, although compileHandler documents that it throws HandlerError for bad handlers.
findings.failure_scenario: A parsed handler such as `where: {hits: {gt: NaN}}` (YAML `.nan`) or `in: [Infinity]` passes every type check, because typeof is 'number'. It then fails at the hash step with a raw TypeError. Callers that catch only HandlerError to report a refused handler crash instead.

findings.summary: `capture.group` is checked only as a non-negative integer, not against the number of groups in the regex.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: {n: {field: head, regex: 'foo(\\d+)', group: 2}}` compiles. `found?.[2]` is always undefined, so the capture is silently never set and `$n` conditions or `${n}` emits are silently absent.

findings.summary: `capture.group` is checked only for being a non-negative integer, not against the regex's number of groups, so an out-of-range group silently gives an absent capture.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: {id: {field: command, regex: 'bd-(\d+)', group: 2}}` compiles, and `${id}` is absent on every row with no error.

findings.summary: `capture.group` is checked only to be a non-negative integer, never against the number of groups in the regex, so a group index past the last group yields an always-absent capture.
findings.failure_scenario: `capture: {id: {field: command, regex: 'bd close (\S+)', group: 2}}` compiles; `found[2]` is always undefined so `id` is never captured and every `${id}` field / `$id` condition is silently absent/false.

findings.summary: `capture.group` is described as 'a whole number' but only `< 0` is checked, so 1.5 and NaN are accepted. The same gap exists for `window.at_least` at line 654.
findings.failure_scenario: `group: 1.5` makes `found[1.5]` undefined, so the capture is never set and every `$name` or template reference to it is silently absent. `at_least: 1.5` requires 2 matches, so a count of 1 never satisfies it. The file elsewhere refuses these non-integers (calls, from), so this is the silent-never-true class.

findings.summary: `capture.group` is only checked for `>= 0`, not for being an integer or for being within the regex's group count.
findings.failure_scenario: `group: 2` on a regex with one group, or `group: 1.5`, gives `found[group]` undefined. The capture is never set and every `$name`/`${name}` is silently absent. NaN passes the `< 0` check too.

findings.summary: `capture.group` is only checked to be a non-negative integer, not against the regex's number of capturing groups, so an out-of-range group silently never captures.
findings.failure_scenario: capture {x: {field: head, regex: 'a(b)', group: 2}} compiles, and `found[2]` is always undefined, so $x is always absent and `where: {$x: {exists: true}}` matches nothing.

findings.summary: `capture.group` is only checked to be a non-negative integer. It is never checked against the number of groups in the compiled regex.
findings.failure_scenario: The capture `{field: command, regex: 'foo (\w+)', group: 2}` compiles. At run time `found[2]` is undefined, so the capture is never set and every `${name}` is silently absent. This is the silent never-true class the file says it refuses.

findings.summary: `capture.regex.exec(source)` runs on the full field, while every other regex use goes through `test()`, which caps the subject at MAX_SUBJECT_LENGTH. The documented ReDoS bound does not hold for captures.
findings.failure_scenario: A capture regex with a pathological pattern run on a multi-megabyte `text` or `path` field is applied to the whole string. The 'at most MAX_SUBJECT_LENGTH characters per event' bound stated at line 43 is violated. The `matches` and `each` paths are capped, so they are the specification.

findings.summary: `emitScope` calls `lastBefore.get(key)` lazily each time it is read, instead of using the `earlier` value captured at trigger time (line 1247). Window rows are rendered later.

When T1's window closes, `${before.x}` resolves to B2, which came after the trigger. After `finish()` clears `lastBefore`, it resolves to absent. The row reports a different reference than the one that existed at the trigger.

findings.summary: `emitScope` looks up `lastBefore.get(key)` each time a template reads it instead of using the `earlier` value captured at the trigger, so a window row shows whatever before-match was newest when the window closed.

The counter and the row disagree.

findings.summary: `emitScope` re-reads `lastBefore.get(key)` lazily when the row is built. The `earlier` value computed at trigger time is ignored.
findings.failure_scenario: A window-mode handler triggers at T1 with before-event B1. A newer matching event B2 arrives before the window closes, so the row is built later and `${before.x}` reads B2. `unsatisfiedBefore` was decided against B1. If `finish()` has cleared `lastBefore`, the field is silently absent. `withBefore(scope, earlier)` should be used.

findings.summary: `emitScope` reads `lastBefore.get(key)` when the row renders instead of using the `earlier` value captured at trigger time, so a window row reports the latest before-match at close time.
findings.failure_scenario: Trigger T with before-match A open in a window, then a new before-match B arrives before the window closes. The row's `${before.file}` shows B's file instead of A's. `lastBefore` is also cleared in `finish`, so the value can even become absent.

findings.summary: `encodeSegment` is not injective: `Buffer.from(name,'utf8')` maps every unpaired surrogate to U+FFFD, so two distinct names collapse into one directory, and the read-side partition guard re-applies the same lossy function so it structurally cannot detect the collision.
findings.failure_scenario: Appending a line with scheme `'\uD800'` and then one with scheme `'�'` puts both in `annotations/%EF%BF%BD/`, and `readRecordTree` returns BOTH lines with no error — the guard compares the on-disk directory to `directoryOf(line)[1]`, which re-applies the same lossy encoding, so both lines 'match' the merged partition. Reachable through `parseCorpus`, since a JSON `"\ud800"` escape in a hand-written or hand-edited corpus is exactly the input this layer documents itself as reading.

findings.summary: `encodeSegment` is not total over names the store accepts: percent-encoding triples non-ASCII byte length, so a legal CJK scheme name overflows NAME_MAX and throws mid-write, leaving a partially written tree.
findings.failure_scenario: A scheme name of 29 CJK characters is accepted by `requireName` and by `annotation_schemes`' own `CHECK (name <> '')`, but encodes to 261 characters and `mkdirSync` throws `ENAMETOOLONG`. Measured threshold: 28 such characters (84 bytes -> 252 encoded) writes; 29 (87 bytes -> 261) throws. Pure ASCII: 255 characters OK, 256 throws. Because the throw is on the write path, a run that has already appended records dies partway through.

findings.summary: `eq` against a `$reference` to an array field passes the type check (array === array), but `===` compares identity, so a window condition comparing arrays is always false (and `ne` always true).
findings.failure_scenario: Window `where: {argv: {eq: $argv}}` never matches a later event that has an identical argv, so every window is reported as noMatch or unclosed.

findings.summary: `eq` and `ne` disagree when the field and the operand are both absent. `eq` compares `undefined === undefined` and is true, and `ne` treats an absent field as always unequal, so both are true at once.
findings.failure_scenario: `where: {path: '$target'}` where the trigger lacks `target` and the event lacks `path`. `eq` matches on undefined === undefined. `{path: {ne: '$target'}}` also matches. A missing value on both sides therefore counts as a match for `eq`, and as a mismatch for `ne`.

findings.summary: `eq` compares with `===` without an absent check, so when a `$capture` failed to match (undefined) and the event field is also absent, undefined === undefined gives true, while `ne` explicitly treats absent as not-equal.
findings.failure_scenario: Take a window where `{path: $file}` where the capture `file` did not match the trigger, and the following event has no path. The condition is true and the window decides on an unrelated event.

findings.summary: `eq`, `ne` and `in` accept a string operand against any field type, so a type mismatch passes compile and is never true.
findings.failure_scenario: `count: '5'` or `in: ['5']` against a number field passes the check and never matches (`===`). `ne` is always true. An array-literal `eq` against an array field is compared by reference and never matches either.

findings.summary: `eq`/`ne` accept an array operand for an array field and compile to `===` on arrays, which is reference equality.
findings.failure_scenario: `where: {argv: {eq: ['a','b']}}` on an event with `argv: ['a','b']`. Both sides are typed 'array', so the type check at line 371 passes and the test is `value === right.get(trigger)`, which is never true for two distinct arrays. The handler compiles and silently matches nothing. `ne` is always true. This is the silent never-true class the file says it refuses. `in` on an array field (line 412) has the same problem: `in: [['a']]` passes the type check but `Set.has` compares by reference.

findings.summary: `eq`/`ne` on an array-typed field (e.g. `command.run.argv`) compare by JS reference equality, so `eq` can never match and `ne` is always true, even for identical array contents.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler author writes `where: { argv: { eq: ["ls", "-la"] } }` on a `command.run` handler. compileHandler accepts it silently (the type-check at line ~500 passes because both the field and the literal report type 'array'), but at runtime `value === right.get(trigger)` compares the event's argv array against the parsed YAML literal array by object identity, which is never true -- the handler runs green and permanently emits zero rows. Symmetrically, the same handler with `ne` instead of `eq` matches every command.run event regardless of argv, since two different array objects are always `!==`. Confirmed empirically: compiled `{on:'command.run', where:{argv:{eq:['ls','-la']}}, emit:{x:'matched'}}` against an event carrying `argv:['ls','-la']` produces 0 rows; the `ne` variant of the same spec against the same event produces 1 row.

findings.summary: `eq`/`ne` on an array-typed field (the only one is `argv`) compare with `===`, which is reference equality on arrays parsed from separate JSON, so `eq` never matches and `ne` always matches.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler on `command.run` with `where: { argv: { eq: ['bd', 'close'] } }` compiles successfully (typeOf(['bd','close']) is 'array', which equals the field's declared type 'array', so the type check at line 371 passes). At runtime, `value === right.get(trigger)` compares the event's `argv` array object against the literal array parsed from the handler spec -- two different object references -- so the condition is false for every event, including one whose `argv` is exactly `['bd', 'close']`. The handler silently matches zero events forever, which is exactly the 'wrong handler runs green' class this file's header says is refused everywhere ('a handler that matches nothing looks exactly like a handler with nothing to match'). The mirror case, `ne` on the same field, is always true instead, matching every event regardless of its actual `argv`. Every other array-typed comparison operator (`contains`, `any_matches`, `followed_by`, `shares_token`, and `matches`, which explicitly requires a string field) refuses or is defined to work correctly on arrays; `eq`/`ne` are the only operators that accept an array-typed field without any array-specific handling, so the guarded siblings are the specification this pair misses.

findings.summary: `eq`/`ne` on an array-typed field compile successfully but compare with `===`, so `eq` is always false and `ne` is always true.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler writes `where: { argv: { eq: ['bd', 'close', 'a-1'] } }` against `command.run` (argv is `'array'` per event.ts:63). `operand()` (line 307-318) returns `typeOf(['bd','close','a-1']) === 'array'`, which matches `fieldType`, so the type check at line 371 passes and no refusal fires. At runtime (line 377-380) the test is `value === right.get(trigger)` — two different array objects are never `===`-equal, so the condition is silently always false. The mirror bug is worse for `ne` (line 381-384): `absent(value) || value !== right.get(trigger)` is silently always true for any present array field, so a handler intending to exclude a specific argv actually matches every event. The handler loads cleanly, looks correct, and reports zero (or all) matches with no error — exactly the class of bug this file's header comment says it exists to refuse.

findings.summary: `exists` refuses only a number argument. Strings, null, lists and other non-booleans are accepted.
findings.failure_scenario: `exists: 'yes'` or `exists: null`. The test is `absent(value) !== arg`, which is always true for a non-boolean arg, so the condition matches every event, or none, regardless of the field.

findings.summary: `exists` refuses only numbers, so a string, null, or object argument compiles and `absent(x) !== arg` is always true.
findings.failure_scenario: where: {subagent_type: {exists: 'false'}} matches every event, including ones where the field is present.

findings.summary: `exists` refuses only numbers, so a string, null, or other non-boolean argument is accepted and the test becomes a constant.
findings.failure_scenario: where: {path: {exists: 'yes'}} compiles; `absent(v) !== 'yes'` is always true, so every event matches whether or not the field is present.

findings.summary: `exists` refuses only numeric args, so a string or other non-boolean passes.
findings.failure_scenario: `exists: 'false'` or `exists: null` (a YAML slip) compiles. `absent(value) !== arg` is then always true, so the condition matches every event whether or not the field exists.

findings.summary: `finish()` counts every still-open window as `unclosed` and discards it without going through `close()`, so a `count` window that already reached `at_least` loses its row.
findings.failure_scenario: With `scope: session`, `until: review.done` and `count: {on: x}, at_least: 1`, if 5 matching events arrive and the replay stops before `review.done`, `finish()` adds 1 to `unclosed` and emits nothing. `unclosed` is documented as a `count` below `at_least`, but here the threshold was met. The same happens for stream scope when the transcript has no session.end. `close()` would have emitted the row.

findings.summary: `followed_by` skips the first array element (`index > 0`), and the arity check accepts more than two items.
findings.failure_scenario: argv ['--status','in_progress'] with `followed_by: ['--status','in_progress']` is false because index 0 is excluded. `followed_by: [a,b,c]` is accepted although the message says 'two strings', and c is ignored.

findings.summary: `found.index >= last` pushes an empty literal string before a reference at position 0, so a template made of exactly one reference has 2 parts and the omit-when-absent branch (line 573) never runs.
findings.failure_scenario: emit `{hits: '${hits}'}` with hits absent produces `hits: ''` instead of leaving the field out; `${before.path}` with no before match also emits `prior: ''` (failing tests 'omits a field whose single reference is absent' and several before: tests).

findings.summary: `gt/gte/lt/lte` check only the field type, not the operand type.
findings.failure_scenario: `gt: '10'` or `gte: [1]` on a number field compiles. At runtime `typeof bound === 'number'` fails, so the condition is silently never true.

findings.summary: `gte` is implemented as `a > b`, identical to `gt`.
findings.failure_scenario: `{hits: {gte: 3}}` on an event with hits 3 evaluates false, so boundary events are silently dropped.

findings.summary: `handlerTokens` documents 'at least 4 long' and the tests assume 4, but the regex is `{5,}`.
findings.failure_scenario: shares_token between 'cli.ts' and a path containing 'main' or 'test'-length tokens finds no overlap. A 4-character token such as 'core' is never a token, so shares_token returns false where 4-character tokens should overlap.

findings.summary: `handlerTokens` documents and is tested as 'at least 4 long', but the regex is `{5,}`.
findings.failure_scenario: The path '/p/cli.ts' shares the 4-character token 'core', so `shares_token` should match a later search for 'core module'. With `{5,}` the 4-character token is dropped and the comparison is false. The result is a wrongly emitted `absent` row (for example read.unused).

findings.summary: `in` (and `eq`/`ne` via `{eq: [...]}`) accept array (or object) literals when the field type is `array`, but compare with Set.has / `===` reference identity, so the condition can never be true (and `ne` always true).
findings.failure_scenario: `where: {argv: {eq: ['git','push']}}` or `{argv: {in: [['git','push']]}}` passes the type check (typeOf 'array' === field type 'array') and silently matches nothing.

findings.summary: `in` guards with `arg.length < 0`, which is always false, so an empty list compiles into a condition that is never true. The sibling window.any guard at line 668 correctly checks `length === 0`.
findings.failure_scenario: where {head: {in: []}} compiles, and the handler never matches any event, with no error.

findings.summary: `in` on an array-typed field builds a `Set` of literal arrays and calls `.has()` on the event's array value, which also relies on reference equality and so never matches.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with `where: { argv: { in: [['bd', 'close'], ['bd', 'update']] } }` compiles (each element of the `in` list has `typeOf` 'array', matching the field's declared type 'array', so the per-element check at lines 411-417 passes). At runtime `allowed.has(left(event, trigger))` does a `Set` lookup with reference equality: the event's own `argv` array is never the same object as any of the literal arrays in `allowed`, so the condition is false for every event no matter what `argv` actually contains -- another silent-zero handler that loads and runs cleanly. Same root cause as the `eq`/`ne` finding at line 371: no operator that accepts an array-typed field guards against structural (vs. reference) comparison here, while the operators purpose-built for arrays (`contains`, `any_matches`, `followed_by`, `shares_token`) compare individual string elements instead and work correctly.

findings.summary: `judged` names, capture names and `each.as` are validated against `/^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]*$/`, but `emit` keys are not validated. `fields` is a plain object, so `__proto__` is silently dropped.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: {__proto__: "${path}"}` compiles. `fields['__proto__'] = value` sets the prototype (a string is ignored) and no field is emitted. Keys with odd characters also pass through unchecked, unlike `judged`.

findings.summary: `maxRecordsPerFile` is injectable and unvalidated, so a value of 0 or negative consumes file index 0001 without ever creating it and starts a fresh tree at 0002.
findings.failure_scenario: `openRecordWriter(root, { maxRecordsPerFile: 0 })` then two appends returns `['entries/note/0002.jsonl', 'entries/note/0003.jsonl']`: `inspect` reports `{index: 1, records: 0}` for a fresh directory and `head.records >= maxRecords` is already true, so the roll fires before the first write. Same for -1. No data loss, but an off-by-one on a public option, and a caller computing the option from a size budget can silently land on 0 and get one file per record.

findings.summary: `merge=union` duplicates a byte-identical record derived independently on two branches, and `readRecordTree` neither dedupes nor reports it, so the corpus silently holds the same entry twice.
findings.failure_scenario: Two branches each append the SAME derived entry line to the SAME partition file, at different positions relative to same-type private records (branch a: [SHARED, hand:a-1]; branch b: [hand:b-1, SHARED]). Merge succeeds with exit 0 and no conflict, and the merged `entries/<type>/0001.jsonl` holds the SHARED line twice. Independently reproduced by the main session with real git: `grep -c 'derived:sess:key-1'` returns `2` on the merged file. `readRecordTree` returns the line twice; downstream `recordEntry` (recorder.ts:263) throws `DuplicateEntryError`. This is the product's central mechanism: two clones ingesting the same transcript derive the same derived-id entries.

findings.summary: `open.delete(key)` on `session.end` runs for every scope, so under `scope: session` it throws away the windows the loop above deliberately kept open, and nothing counts them.
findings.failure_scenario: scope: session, events [file.changed(main), session.end(sub), check.run(sub)]: the window is deleted at the sub stream's end, so the check.run produces no row and finish() counts unclosed 0. The test 'does not let a stream's session.end close a session-scoped window' expects 1 row.

findings.summary: `open.delete(key)` on `session.end` runs whatever the scope is, so under `scope: session` the first stream's end silently discards every open window in the session, with no row and no `unclosed` count.
findings.failure_scenario: Session scope with `until: agent.return`. A subagent file ends before the `agent.return` arrives. Every pending window disappears, and `finish()` counts 0 unclosed, so the result is a silent loss.

findings.summary: `partition` returns `event.session_id` in both branches, so `scope: stream` no longer partitions by `(session_id, agent_id)` as documented at lines 1013-1014 and 1050-1053.
findings.failure_scenario: A session has a main stream (agent A) and a subagent stream (agent B). With the default stream scope, B's events land in A's open windows, `running` set and `lastBefore`. A `first` window opened by A's trigger is matched or closed by B's events. B's `session.end` runs `open.delete(key)` and closes A's windows early with closed_by 'session.end'. Rows are wrong or lost, and the seq comparisons mix two sequences.

findings.summary: `partition` returns `event.session_id` on both branches, so under `scope: stream` the key is the session, not `(session_id, agent_id)` as the docs and event.ts require.
findings.failure_scenario: A main stream and a subagent stream share a session_id. A trigger in main opens a window. Events from the subagent (different seq/call numbering) are offered to it, and the subagent's `session.end` deletes main's open windows and running set. Windows close on the wrong stream's `until`, `calls` bound or `session.end`, and `before:` references leak across agents. The `session` branch should be `session_id`. The `stream` branch should be `session_id` plus `agent_id` with a separator.

findings.summary: `past` uses `event.call >= limit`, but an event whose call equals the limit is still inside the window (doc: 'at most trigger.call + N').
findings.failure_scenario: calls: 1, trigger call 1, limit 2. A count event at call 2 is treated as past the limit and closes the window, so the straggler test's expected count of 1 is not reached.

findings.summary: `pathType` accepts `argv.0` (`/^\d+$/`) although `read` is 1-based (`Number(part) - 1`), and `rest.length > 1` lets one extra segment through (`argv.1.x`).
findings.failure_scenario: `where: { 'argv.0': 'bd' }` compiles, but `read` looks at index -1 and always gets undefined, so the condition is silently never true. `argv.1.x` also compiles and always reads undefined.

findings.summary: `pathType` allows extra path segments past the index (`rest.length > 1` instead of `> 0`).
findings.failure_scenario: `argv.1.x` is accepted as a string-typed path, but `read` returns undefined for it at run time, so the condition is silently never true.

findings.summary: `pathType` relies on `eventFieldType`, which indexes plain objects (`ENVELOPE_FIELDS[field] ?? EVENT_KINDS[kind]?.[field]`). Inherited names such as `constructor`, `toString` or `__proto__` therefore resolve as fields.
findings.failure_scenario: An `emit` of `${toString}` or `${constructor}` compiles, because the type is a function rather than `undefined`. At run time `read` returns `Object.prototype.toString` and the row contains `function toString() { [native code] }`. `where: {constructor: ...}` is refused with a misleading type message instead of 'no field'. The compile-time typo guard is bypassed. Elsewhere the file uses `Object.hasOwn` for the same registries.

findings.summary: `pathType` resolves field names through `eventFieldType`, which indexes plain objects, so inherited names like `constructor`, `toString` and `__proto__` count as valid fields. The kind and filter lookups in this file use `Object.hasOwn`, but this one does not.
findings.failure_scenario: `emit: {c: '${constructor}'}` or `where: {constructor: {exists: true}}` compiles, because `ENVELOPE_FIELDS['constructor']` is `Object`, which is not undefined. At run time `read(event,'constructor')` returns `Object` from the prototype, so the row carries the text 'function Object() { [native code] }' and `exists: true` is always true. Capture names and `each.as` such as `toString` are refused with a misleading 'shadows the trigger's own field' message. Compare `Object.hasOwn(EVENT_KINDS, on)` at line 793 and `Object.hasOwn(FILTERS, filter)` at line 551.

findings.summary: `read` indexes arrays with `Number(part) - 1`, but paths are 0-based (`argv.1` means the second element), so every indexed path reads the wrong element and `argv.0` reads index -1.
findings.failure_scenario: where `{'argv.1': 'close'}` on argv ['bd','close','a-1'] reads 'bd' and never matches; the 'fans out one row per matching array element' test gets [] instead of two rows.

findings.summary: `read` resolves an array index path with `Number(part) - 1`, making `argv.N` one-based, but the tests and the `pathType` doc treat `argv.1` as the element at index 1.

The file's purpose is to refuse misspelled or unknown fields, and these go through.

findings.summary: rows() slices the each list at `each.from + 1`, which drops the element at index `from`.
findings.failure_scenario: each {field: argv, from: 2} over ['bd','close','a-1','--x','b-2'] iterates only ['--x','b-2'], so it emits b-2 but drops a-1.

findings.summary: shares_token returns true when the right operand is not a string (line 478) or the left field is absent (line 488), so missing data counts as a match.

findings.summary: shares_token returns true when the right-hand `$ref` is not a string (line 478) or the left field is absent or not string/array (line 488), treating missing data as a match.

findings.summary: stats parses --limit with Number(raw) while every sibling command uses oclif's Flags.integer, so one flag name accepts two different input languages.

findings.summary: unfiltered is computed from 'options.filter === undefined' and never consults the struck narrowing, so with --struck the denominator equals its own numerator.

findings.summary: window.at_least is checked for number >= 1 but not Number.isInteger, unlike window.calls at line 586, despite the error message saying 'whole number'.

findings.summary: window.at_least is not checked with Number.isInteger, unlike window.calls (line 586), although the refusal says 'must be a whole number'.

findings.summary: window.until, window any[].on (678) and before.on (757) validate with `kind in EVENT_KINDS`, which accepts inherited Object.prototype keys, while `on` (793) and window.on (691) use `Object.hasOwn`.

findings.summary: window.until, window any[].on and before.on validate kinds with `in EVENT_KINDS`, which accepts inherited prototype keys, while the sibling checks at lines 691 and 793 use Object.hasOwn.

findings.summary: withBefore intercepts any name starting with 'before' (no dot) and is applied even when the handler declares no before:, so captures or each.as names like 'before_path' always resolve to undefined.
findings.failure_scenario: capture: {before_path: {field: command, regex: '(\S+)'}} with emit p: '${before_path}' and no before: key: compile succeeds but every row has p absent/empty because withBefore returns undefined for the name.

findings.summary: withBefore is documented to return the scope itself when the handler has no before:, but it always returns a wrapper. Any `before.`-prefixed name therefore resolves to undefined instead of going to the trigger scope.
findings.failure_scenario: A handler with no before: and a capture/each item named with a 'before.' prefix cannot occur because of the name regex, but the documented byte-identical-path guarantee for old handlers does not hold.

findings.summary: withBefore's doc promises it returns `scope` itself when the handler declares no before:, but it always returns a wrapper, so pre-existing handlers do not run through the same function as claimed.
findings.failure_scenario: Handler without before: every trigger scope is wrapped; any `before.`-prefixed name is intercepted and returns undefined rather than going to the trigger scope, contrary to the documented identity guarantee.
